reviewNote: [REVIEW] Draft written from standard milling practice because the pocketbook PDF was not available. Parameters quoted in the build plan (40–50 psi sterilisation, oil in fibre < 5%) are from the pocketbook; everything else needs expert sign-off.

stations.name: FFB Reception
stations.purpose: Fresh fruit bunches (FFB) arrive by lorry, are weighed, graded for ripeness and quality, and stored on a sloping loading ramp until they go into the steriliser cages. Good grading here protects OER downstream, because unripe or rotten bunches cannot be fixed later.
howItWorks: Lorries are weighed in and out on the weighbridge to get the net FFB weight.
Graders sample loads and sort bunches by ripeness (unripe, under-ripe, ripe, over-ripe, empty, rotten, long stalk).
Loads are tipped into ramp bays with hydraulic doors.
Bunches slide by gravity from the ramp into steriliser cages (horizontal) or a conveyor (vertical/continuous steriliser).
Loose fruit is collected separately because it carries high oil and FFA.

keyEquipment.name: Loading ramp
keyEquipment.size: Bays with hydraulic doors, about 1 day storage

keyParameters.name: FFB processed within
keyParameters.target: 24 h of harvest (FFA rises with delay)

commonProblems.cause: Old or bruised FFB, long ramp storage
commonProblems.action: Process first-in-first-out; enforce harvest-to-mill time.
Tighten grading; give feedback to estates / dealers.
Clean daily; check hydraulic pressure.

quiz.q: Why must FFB be processed quickly after harvest?
quiz.explain: Bruised fruit activates lipase, which splits oil into free fatty acids.

quiz.q: What does the weighbridge give the mill?
quiz.explain: Gross minus tare gives net FFB, the basis for OER and KER.

quiz.q: Which bunch class should be rejected or penalised?
options: Over-ripe with a few loose fruits
quiz.explain: Rotten bunches give high FFA and little oil.

stations.name: Sterilisation
stations.purpose: Bunches are cooked with saturated steam under pressure. This stops the lipase enzyme that raises FFA, loosens fruitlets from the bunch so they can be threshed, softens the mesocarp for pressing, and conditions nuts so kernels come loose from the shell.
howItWorks: Cages are pushed into a horizontal pressure vessel and the door is closed.
Steam is admitted in three peaks (triple-peak cycle). Each release drives out air, which would otherwise insulate the fruit.
Pressure is held at about 40–45 psi (≈3 bar g) for the cooking period.
Condensate is drained throughout; it carries some oil to the effluent.
Final blow-off depressurises the vessel and the cages are pulled out to the tippler.

keyEquipment.name: Horizontal steriliser
keyEquipment.size: Ø 2.1–2.7 m, 2–4 cages, 3 bar g design

keyEquipment.name: Steam inlet, exhaust and condensate valves

commonProblems.cause: Short cooking, air not purged, low pressure
commonProblems.action: Check peak sequence and holding time; check steam supply.
Reduce holding time; keep cycle to design.
Recover condensate oil; review cycle.

quiz.q: Why use three steam peaks?
options: To drive air out of the vessel
quiz.explain: Air is a poor conductor of heat; purging it lets steam reach the bunch core.

quiz.q: Typical cooking pressure is about:
quiz.explain: The pocketbook gives 40–50 psi.

quiz.q: Over-sterilisation mainly harms:
quiz.explain: Long cooking oxidises the oil and lowers DOBI.

stations.name: Threshing
stations.purpose: Sterilised bunches are tumbled in a rotating drum so the loosened fruitlets fall out through the bars, leaving the empty fruit bunch (EFB). Fruitlets go to the digester; EFB goes to the incinerator, mulching or a biomass plant.
howItWorks: A hopper and auto-feeder deliver bunches evenly into the drum.
The drum turns at about 22–24 rpm, lifting and dropping bunches so fruitlets break off.
Fruitlets fall through gaps between the drum bars onto a conveyor.
EFB exits the end of the drum; some mills pass it through a second thresher or EFB press.
A fruit elevator lifts the fruitlets to the digester.

commonProblems.action: Fix steriliser cycle; feed evenly; recycle USB.
Check cycle; consider EFB press.
Check rpm against design.

quiz.q: What leaves the end of the thresher drum?
quiz.explain: Fruitlets fall through the bars; EFB exits the end.

quiz.q: Typical thresher drum speed:
quiz.explain: Fast enough to lift and drop bunches, slow enough not to bruise fruit.

quiz.q: Unstripped bunches usually point to a problem in:
quiz.explain: Under-cooked bunches hold their fruit.

stations.name: Digestion & Pressing
stations.purpose: Fruitlets are mashed in a heated digester to break the oil cells, then squeezed in a twin-screw press. The press gives crude oil (oil, water and solids) and a press cake of fibre and nuts.
howItWorks: The digester (a steam-jacketed vessel with stirring arms) turns the fruit into a hot mash at about 90–95 °C.
Mash drops into the twin-screw press; cones at the outlet set the back pressure.
Crude oil drains through the press cage into the crude oil gutter, then through the sand trap tank and circular (vibrating) screens to the crude oil tanks.
Hot water is added to dilute the crude oil (diluted crude oil, DCO) so it separates well.
Press cake goes to the cake breaker conveyor and the nut/fibre separator.

keyEquipment.name: Vibrating screen and sand trap tank

commonProblems.cause: Low cone pressure, worn screws, poor digestion
commonProblems.action: Raise cone pressure; check digester level and temperature; replace worn screws.
Lower cone pressure; balance against oil loss.
Keep the digester at least ¾ full.

quiz.q: Why keep the digester full?
options: To give proper mashing and steady press feed
quiz.explain: A full digester gives longer residence and even press feed.

quiz.q: Raising press cone pressure usually:
options: Lowers oil in fibre but breaks more nuts
quiz.explain: It is a trade-off between oil loss and broken nuts.

quiz.q: Press cake contains mainly:
quiz.explain: Fibre and nuts go to the nut/fibre separation station.

stations.name: Clarification
stations.purpose: Diluted crude oil (DCO) is separated into oil and sludge in two stages. The crude oil tank gives a first split into skimmed oil and sludge; the clarifier tank then recovers the oil left in the sludge. Pure oil is vacuum-dried to become CPO, and the final sludge is centrifuged to recover more oil before going to the effluent ponds.
howItWorks: DCO from the sand trap tank and circular (vibrating) screens flows into the crude oil tanks, which are steam-heated to about 90–95 °C.
In the crude oil tank the oil rises: the top oil is skimmed off to the skimmed oil holding tank, and the bottom sludge goes to the sludge holding tank.
Skimmed oil is pumped straight to the pure oil tank.
Sludge is pumped to the clarifier distribution tank and into the clarifier tank. Oil floats to the top and overflows to the pure oil tank.
The clarifier underflow goes to the sludge tank, then the 2-stage precleaner and sludge separators/decanters recover more oil, which returns to the clarifier.
From the pure oil tank, the CPO pump sends oil through the vacuum dryer (moisture below 0.2%); the oil transfer pump then sends dry CPO to the storage tanks.

keyEquipment.name: Skimmed oil & sludge holding tanks + pumps
Vacuum dryer + float tank, oil transfer pump

commonProblems.cause: Low temperature, poor dilution, overloaded separator
commonProblems.action: Check temperature and dilution ratio; clean separator nozzles.

commonProblems.cause: Vacuum dryer fault, or sludge carried into the pure oil tank
commonProblems.action: Check dryer vacuum and float tank; check skimming level in the crude oil tank and clarifier oil outlet.
Adjust dilution; increase temperature.

commonProblems.symptom: Sludge holding tank overflowing / oil in sludge holding tank
commonProblems.cause: Skimmer set too low in the crude oil tank, or a pump trip
commonProblems.action: Adjust the skimming level; check the holding tank pumps and changeover.

quiz.q: Oil separates in the clarifier because:
options: It is lighter than water and sludge
quiz.explain: Gravity settling: oil (≈0.86 t/m³) floats on water and solids.

quiz.q: What is the vacuum dryer for?
quiz.explain: It lowers moisture so CPO keeps its quality in storage.

quiz.q: The sludge tank is sized on 50% of:
quiz.explain: A pocketbook erratum: it is 50% of crude oil, not FFB.

stations.name: Nut / Fibre Separation
stations.purpose: Press cake is broken up and an air stream lifts the light fibre away from the heavy nuts. Fibre is the main boiler fuel. Nuts go to polishing and cracking.
howItWorks: A cake breaker conveyor breaks up the press cake and dries it slightly.
In the de-pericarper column, an air stream from a fan lifts fibre upward to a cyclone.
Nuts fall to a polishing drum that removes remaining fibre.
Fibre from the cyclone goes to the boiler fuel conveyor.
A de-stoner removes stones and heavy debris from the nuts pneumatically.

keyParameters.name: Nuts carried into fibre
keyParameters.target: Minimal: check the fibre cyclone outlet

commonProblems.action: Close the damper slightly.

commonProblems.cause: Air velocity too low; wet cake
commonProblems.action: Open damper; check cake breaker.
Regulate feed; check fan belts.

quiz.q: What separates fibre from nuts?
quiz.explain: Fibre is light and is carried up by air; nuts fall.

quiz.q: Correct air density at 27 °C for sizing:
quiz.explain: 1.777 is a misprint in the pocketbook.

quiz.q: Fibre is mainly used as:
quiz.explain: Fibre is the main boiler fuel, with shell as a supplement.

stations.name: Kernel Recovery
stations.purpose: Nuts are cracked and the kernels are separated from the shells, then dried and stored. Kernel is the second product of the mill, measured as KER.
howItWorks: Nuts are conditioned (dried or graded) so the kernel shrinks from the shell.
A ripple mill or centrifugal cracker breaks the shell.
A winnowing column removes light shell fragments with air.
A clay bath or hydrocyclone separates kernel from heavier shell by density.
Kernels are dried in silos to about 7% moisture and stored in bulk.

commonProblems.action: Adjust gap; replace rotor bars.

commonProblems.cause: Winnowing air too strong, hydrocyclone setting
commonProblems.action: Adjust damper and cyclone pressure.
Check silo heater and air flow.

quiz.q: A ripple mill is used to:
quiz.explain: The rotor bars throw nuts against a ripple plate to crack them.

quiz.q: Hydrocyclones separate kernel from shell by:
quiz.explain: Shell is denser than kernel.

quiz.q: Typical stored kernel moisture:
quiz.explain: Drying to about 7% stops mould and FFA rise in the kernel.

stations.name: Boiler & Engine Room
stations.purpose: The mill makes its own steam and power from biomass. A water-tube boiler burns fibre and shell; high-pressure steam drives a back-pressure turbine for electricity, and the exhaust steam (about 3 bar g) is used for sterilisation and heating.
howItWorks: Fibre and shell are fed to the furnace; induced and forced draught fans control combustion.
Treated feed water is heated in the boiler to make steam at 20–30 bar g.
Steam drives a back-pressure turbine coupled to an alternator.
Turbine exhaust steam goes to the back pressure vessel (BPV) at ≈3 bar g and on to the steriliser and process.
A diesel genset covers start-up and low-crop periods.

commonProblems.cause: Too much fuel, too little air, wet fibre
commonProblems.action: Balance fuel feed and draught; dry fibre.
Check fuel mix (add shell); soot-blow; clean tubes.
Shed load; stabilise boiler.

quiz.q: Why use a back-pressure turbine?
options: Its exhaust steam is used for processing
quiz.explain: The mill needs low-pressure steam, so it generates power on the way down.

quiz.q: Main boiler fuels in a palm oil mill:
quiz.explain: Press fibre and shell are burned; EFB is wetter and harder to burn.

quiz.q: Correcting PF from 0.55 to 0.95 needs a multiplier of:
quiz.explain: tan(acos 0.55) − tan(acos 0.95) = 1.190. The pocketbook table misprints 1.490.

stations.name: Effluent (POME) Treatment
stations.purpose: Palm oil mill effluent (POME) is hot, acidic and very high in organic matter. It is cooled, oil is recovered, and it is treated biologically in anaerobic and aerobic stages until it meets DOE discharge limits or is used for land application. Biogas from the anaerobic stage can be captured for energy.
howItWorks: Sludge, condensate and hydrocyclone water flow to a fat pit / oil trap where floating oil is skimmed.
Cooling and mixing ponds bring the temperature down.
Anaerobic ponds or closed digesters break down most of the BOD and produce biogas (methane).
Facultative and aerobic ponds (often with aerators) polish the effluent.
Final effluent is discharged or used for land application, under DOE licence conditions.

commonProblems.action: Reduce loading; recirculate; desludge.
Desludge ponds; add aeration or polishing plant.
Improve sludge separator and fat pit skimming.

quiz.q: Which stage produces biogas?
quiz.explain: Methanogenic bacteria in the anaerobic stage produce methane.

quiz.q: Raw POME BOD is roughly:
quiz.explain: POME is about 100 times stronger than domestic sewage.

quiz.q: Who sets mill effluent discharge limits in Malaysia?
quiz.explain: The Department of Environment (DOE) licenses mill discharges.
